Automatic Generation of Beginner-Friendly Ukulele Chord Arrangements

Panshul ai23btech11018@iith.ac.in                

Madhava ai23btech11007@iith.ac.in

1 [[Background and Motivation]]  
Suppose a beginner wants to play “Hey, Soul Sister” on the ukulele. The chord progression commonly used for the song can be represented as E → B → C#m → A. For a beginner, some of these chord shapes may be uncomfortable to play. However, the same harmonic progression can be represented in another key. For example, transposing it down by four semitones gives C → G → Am → F, which provides a simple motivating example of how the representation of a song can affect playability.

  

![](data:image/png;base64,)  
  
Learning to accompany a song on an instrument therefore involves more than identifying its chord sequence. Automatic Chord Estimation from audio is already an established Music Information Retrieval problem, with extensive work on features, models, datasets, and evaluation methods [1]. The proposed project focuses on the subsequent problem: how an estimated chord progression can be transformed into a beginner-friendly ukulele arrangement.  
Several possible transformations will be investigated, including transposition, chord simplification, chord substitution, and ukulele-specific voicing selection. The extent to which these transformations preserve the essential harmonic structure of the song remains an empirical question to be investigated.

2 [[Problem Statement]]

Given a song recording, such as a YouTube song, generate a time-synchronized ukulele chord arrangement that is easier for a beginner to play while preserving the essential harmonic structure of the original song.

  

3 [[Related Work ]]

[1] McVicar et al. (2014), “Automatic Chord Estimation from Audio: A Review of the State of the Art.” Reviews the established Automatic Chord Estimation problem, including feature extraction, modelling strategies, training datasets, and evaluation. This supports the use of existing chord-estimation methods as a project component rather than reproducing the ACE literature.

[2] Vélez Vásquez et al. (ISMIR 2023), “Quantifying the Ease of Playing Song Chords on the Guitar.” Introduces a seven-criterion guitar playability rubric, annotates 200 songs from the McGill Billboard dataset using a guitar expert, and evaluates automatic rule-based and deep-learning prediction of playability. The study is explicitly focused on rhythm guitar.

Other works haven’t been explored right  now 

The directly related work identified here focuses on guitar rather than ukulele [2]. The proposed project will therefore investigate how an analogous arrangement problem can be formulated for a four-string ukulele. The effects of ukulele tuning, available voicings, fretboard constraints, and beginner-oriented playability criteria have not yet been established within this project and will be treated as questions for investigation rather than as predetermined assumptions.

  

4. [[Proposed System  ]]
Song audio → existing chord estimation → chord timeline → candidate arrangements → ukulele playability evaluation → recommended arrangement

5.[[Datasets]] 
Existing chord-annotated datasets can be used to evaluate the arrangement stage without requiring a new chord-transcription dataset. For example, the McGill Billboard dataset was used by Vélez Vásquez et al. as the source of 200 songs for guitar playability annotation [2]. 

A separate ukulele-specific playability dataset is not assumed to exist for this project. If required, a small human evaluation can be collected to assess whether automatically generated arrangements agree with perceived beginner playability. The need, size, and annotation protocol for such a dataset are pending investigation.

6. [[Evaluation]] 

The generated arrangements will be evaluated from three perspectives:

- Playability: Quantitative measures such as finger count, fret span, barre chords, chord-transition difficulty, and number of chord changes.
    
- Harmonic fidelity: Measure how well the simplified arrangement preserves the original chord progression and harmonic structure.
    
- Human evaluation: Ask ukulele players to rate the generated arrangements for ease of playing and perceived musical similarity to the original.
    

7. [[Potential Contributions]]

The project aims to contribute, even incrementally, to automatic beginner-oriented ukulele arrangement:

• Ukulele-specific playability rubric: Extend existing chord-playability criteria to the ukulele.

• Human playability annotations: Collect a small set of human judgements to evaluate and refine the proposed rubric.

• Chord simplification strategies: Systematically explore transposition, capo selection, chord simplification, substitution and others.

• Automatic arrangement pipeline: Integrate chord estimation, candidate generation, playability scoring, and arrangement selection into one system.

• Empirical evaluation: Study which simplification strategies improve playability while retaining the essential harmonic structure of the song. 

The goal is not necessarily a major methodological breakthrough, but to make a small, well-evaluated contribution toward understanding and automating beginner-friendly ukulele arrangements.

8. [[Key References]]

[1] M. McVicar, R. Santos-Rodriguez, Y. Ni, and T. De Bie, “Automatic Chord Estimation from Audio: A Review of the State of the Art,” IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing, vol. 22, no. 2, pp. 556–575, 2014. DOI: 10.1109/TASLP.2013.2294580.

[2] M. A. Vélez Vásquez, M. Baelemans, J. Driedger, W. Zuidema, and J. A. Burgoyne, “Quantifying the Ease of Playing Song Chords on the Guitar,” Proceedings of ISMIR 2023, pp. 725–732, 2023. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.10265391.

9. What Remains Incomplete

Literature survey: Read and synthesize additional work on chord estimation, chord simplification, instrument-specific playability, and music arrangement.

Ukulele playability: Determine which playability criteria and voicing constraints are actually relevant to beginner ukulele players.

Arrangement strategies: Study and compare the possible simplification and optimization strategies, including their interactions and trade-offs.

Evaluation: Finalize the human-annotation protocol, evaluation criteria, and baseline arrangements needed to validate the proposed approach.

System design: Finalize the candidate-generation, playability-scoring, and arrangement-selection methodology based on the findings above.

These aspects are intentionally left open at the proposal stage and will be finalized after further literature review and initial experimentation.

10 Appendix 

![](data:image/png;base64,)

[[Possible Ukulele Arrangement Optimizations]]  


The following are candidate operations to be explored. Their usefulness, relative importance, and interaction have not yet been established and will be treated as pending work.

Global transposition: Shift the entire progression to another key with potentially easier ukulele chord shapes.

Capo selection: Use easier chord shapes while retaining the desired sounding key.

Chord extension removal: For example, simplify Am7 to Am or Cmaj7 to C when appropriate.

Chord substitution: Replace an awkward chord with a harmonically compatible simpler alternative.

Passing-chord removal: Remove brief transitional chords when the main harmonic movement can be preserved.

Chord-change reduction: Reduce closely spaced changes to lower playing demands.

Voicing selection: Choose among multiple ukulele realizations of the same chord.

Transition optimization: Prefer consecutive voicings with lower estimated finger movement.

Finger-count optimization: Prefer voicings requiring fewer simultaneously fretted fingers.

Stretch minimization: Penalize large fret spans or uncomfortable finger stretches.

Barre-chord avoidance: Potentially penalize or avoid barre chords for beginner arrangements.

Fret-position optimization: Prefer a manageable and consistent fretboard region.

Open-string preference: Investigate whether open-string voicings reduce playing difficulty.

Chord-shape repetition: Investigate whether repeated familiar shapes reduce cognitive and physical demands.

Harmonic-fidelity constraint: Limit simplifications that alter essential harmonic information beyond an acceptable level.

Multi-objective optimization: Balance estimated playability against harmonic fidelity.
